title: The herdr executor behind the five operations
description:
The herdr executor: the five operations, and nothing about herdr above them.

Implement Executor for herdr behind the SAME interface Phase 1 defined
(internal/reconcile/reconcile.go:57): Start, Inspect, CollectDetail, Cancel,
Dispose. All herdr-specific addressing lives inside JobHandle.handle, the one
open object in the contract (internal/exec/subprocess/record.go:218-223). The
reconciler must learn nothing about panes, workspaces or protocols.

Design rules, from the Phase 1 retro:
- THE VERDICT LIVES IN DURABLE EVIDENCE, NEVER IN THE SUBSTRATE. Phase 1's
  executor decides from a report on disk, commits on a branch, and an exit code,
  and refuses to read process chatter as liveness. This one inherits that.
  ticks' own collect package is the proof it works: collect.go:108-109 makes
  zero herdr calls, so herdr cannot touch a verdict by construction. Keep that
  property.
- The substrate goes in PROVENANCE. Records already carry executor, model and
  profile digest; add the herdr protocol and server version, so a run that spans
  an upgrade can be diagnosed rather than guessed at.
- Do NOT port ticks' spawn/wait/reconcile/cleanup packages. ticfac's reconciler
  already owns waves, adoption, disposition and cleanup. Only the herdr-specific
  parts belong here: Start is agent.start plus worktree/workspace creation,
  Inspect is agent.get plus durable evidence, Cancel is the stop, Dispose is the
  teardown. Read those four ticks packages for the hard-won details (the
  pane-busy retry, the readiness poll, the refusal to tear down on an unanswered
  agent.list) and carry the LESSONS, not the code.
- Resume across an upgrade is the first hazard to design for: a job started
  under one protocol that a later leg cannot address is HELD for a person and
  never redispatched — the old worker may still be alive and spending.

## Enforcing the wall clock is THIS executor's job

Noticing a deadline and enforcing one are different jobs, and Phase 1 splits
them across the seam you are implementing.

What you INHERIT and must not re-implement: the settlement deadline is
reconciler-side (dispatch.go:971 — issued + WallSeconds + the wipe threshold),
so a herdr worker that goes quiet is declared settled on schedule exactly as a
local one is. The bound reaches you as spec.Limits.WallSeconds (dispatch.go:717,
default 3600 — "an unbounded job is one nothing stops", reconcile.go:38-39). The
escalation path is inherited too: a worker whose report answers BLOCKED or
NEEDS_CONTEXT is held for a person rather than merged.

What does NOT come for free: the KILL. In Phase 1 the wall clock is enforced
inside the executor, because that executor owns the process it started and can
stop the tree (subprocess/inspect.go:131, collect.go:177). A herdr worker's
process belongs to HERDR. Nothing you inherit stops it. So the reconciler will
correctly declare the attempt settled and move on while the agent keeps running
and keeps spending — the exact failure the bound exists to prevent, made worse
because the run's records will say it is over.

Do:
- Enforce spec.Limits.WallSeconds through herdr: stop the agent when the bound
  is reached, and record that it was stopped at its wall clock rather than that
  it merely settled — the two are different verdicts and Phase 1 already
  distinguishes them.
- If a bound cannot be enforced through the herdr protocol available to you,
  that is a REFUSAL AT DISPATCH naming the bound and the herdr version, not a
  promise. A limit nothing enforces is worse than no limit: it is a limit the
  operator believes in.
- A stop at the wall clock is not a verdict about the WORK. It settles the
  attempt; whatever the branch and the report hold is still read the usual way.
  See tick x6j, which owns that rule.

## The boundary must be ENFORCED by this executor, not requested in a prompt

Seen live on wave 2: the bcv worker committed RESULT-bcv.md onto its attempt
branch. Every other worker in this epic left it untracked, which is what the
teardown expects — archive it to .tick/logs/herd/<epic>/, then remove it. Under
the tk herd ritual nothing PREVENTS the commit; the prompt just asks.

`.tick/learnings.md` already carries the rule, from an earlier incident:

    Problem: A worker committed tracker state although its prompt forbade it.
    Rule:    A boundary the substrate can enforce must not rest on
             instruction-following — make it impossible and REPORT every
             attempt.

Phase 1's subprocess executor implements exactly that, in two layers, and the
herdr executor inherits the OBLIGATION but not the code:

1. PREVENT. Start writes a git exclude for the artifact prefix into the
   worktree BEFORE the runner is launched (git.go excludeFromGit), so an
   ordinary `git add -A` cannot pick the report up. Dispose removes the line
   first, while the worktree it was resolved against still exists, so nothing
   is left behind in info/exclude.
2. DETECT, because prevention is bypassable. Collect re-checks the boundary
   against the branch diff and treats a report found there as a violation
   (collect.go:83, :185-186) — the fixture `force_report` exists precisely to
   drive a runner that does `git add -f` past the exclude. A10 requires the
   attempt be REPORTED, not silently refused: violations are recorded as
   observations and carried into the collected record's boundary_violations.

Do the same here. The mechanism differs — a herdr worker's worktree is created
through herdr rather than by this executor — but the two obligations do not:
the exclude is written before the agent starts, and collect refuses-and-reports
a report or artifact found on the branch. Neither may depend on the worker's
prompt, its cooperation, or which agent kind is running.
notes: 2026-09-10 11:28 - Scope addition from the operator's stall question: enforcing spec.Limits.WallSeconds is this executor's job. The reconciler-side settlement deadline is inherited; the KILL is not, because Phase 1 implements it inside the local executor which owns its own process tree. A bound that cannot be enforced through the available herdr protocol is a refusal at dispatch, not a promise.
acceptance_criteria: A herdr Executor implements Start, Inspect, CollectDetail, Cancel and Dispose; the reconcile package contains no herdr-specific code and the Executor interface is unchanged; all herdr addressing lives inside JobHandle.handle; the verdict is derived from the report and the branch and never from a herdr call, asserted by a test that answers every herdr query with an error and still collects the right verdict; every record a herdr dispatch produces carries the herdr protocol and server version in its provenance; go test -short -timeout 45m ./... green. The executor ENFORCES spec.Limits.WallSeconds through herdr rather than relying on the reconciler's settlement deadline alone: a worker that runs past its bound is actually stopped, and is recorded as stopped at its wall clock rather than merely settled; a test drives a worker past the bound and asserts both the stop and the wording. Where the bound cannot be enforced through the available herdr protocol, dispatch REFUSES naming the bound and the herdr version rather than proceeding with a limit nothing enforces. The artifact boundary is enforced by the executor and never by the prompt: an exclude for the report/artifact prefix is written into the worktree before the agent is started, and removed on dispose while the worktree still exists. Collect independently re-checks the branch diff, so a worker that force-adds its report past the exclude is caught, refused, and REPORTED as a boundary violation carried in the collected record rather than silently dropped. Tests cover both an ordinary add-all (prevented) and a deliberate force-add (detected and reported).
